claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy retains non-equilibrium features such as residual porosity, metastable phases, and chemical heterogeneity.
Elevated-temperature gas exposure degrades the alloy primarily through changes in its native oxide scale.
Oxidizing exposure selectively oxidizes Al and Cr.
The Al/Cr-rich oxide formed under oxidizing conditions is initially protective.
Thermal mismatch and oxide phase transformations destabilize the oxide scale.
Oxide-scale instability causes spallation.
Scale spallation creates stress concentrations that nucleate intergranular cracks.
Reducing exposure suppresses formation of a stable protective oxide scale.
Suppression of the protective scale under reducing conditions enhances atomic diffusion along grain boundaries.
Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion under reducing conditions produces internal voids and grain-boundary decohesion.
Both oxidizing and reducing degradation pathways can culminate in catastrophic failure.
Highly oxidizing exposure will produce oxide-scale thickening followed by spallation relative to the baseline.
Highly oxidizing exposure will increase intergranular crack density and cause premature mechanical failure relative to the baseline.
Reducing exposure will produce grain-boundary void coalescence and mechanical embrittlement relative to the baseline.
Reducing exposure will cause early catastrophic failure.
A chemically inert high-temperature baseline has minimal oxide-scale development and low crack and void densities.
The proposed degradation modes apply at temperatures of at least 700°C for exposures lasting several hours.
The oxidizing degradation mode applies above ambient-air oxygen concentration, exemplified as greater than 21% O2.
The reducing degradation mode applies in H2-rich environments or at oxygen concentrations below 5%.

contradictions.description: Ambient air is proposed as a substantially oxidizing test condition, but the stated applicability boundary requires oxygen above ambient air levels (>21% O2). Thus, the air arm of the proposed experiment may fall outside the hypothesis's own oxidizing boundary.
